                            <div class="hlFld-Fulltext"><div id="abstractId1" class="hlFld-Abstract"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="abstract">Abstract</h2><p class="last">Carousel ads introduce a unique interactive element to in-feed social media advertising by prompting consumers to swipe sideways. Four studies offer novel insights into the “carousel effect” that results from the interactivity and multi-card structure of carousel ads. An exploratory investigation of how consumers perceive and experience carousel ads reveals four experiential themes: curiosity, convenience, perceived control, and immersion. A real-world, mobile eye-tracking study further shows that activated carousel ads significantly increase attention and brand recall compared with other advertising formats, and longer carousel ads enhance attention further. Two additional studies demonstrate that brand attitude drives carousel ad activation, such that consumers are more likely to interact with carousel ads from strong brands. These findings extend perceived control and attitude–behavior consistency theories by identifying psychological mechanisms that underlie the effectiveness of carousel ads. They also offer actionable guidance for marketers seeking to improve the effectiveness of their advertising.</p></div><div class="abstractKeywords"><div class="hlFld-KeywordText"><div><p id="kwd-title-d43339387e130" class="kwd-title">Keywords: </p><ul aria-labelledby="kwd-title-d43339387e130"><li><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/carousel+advertising" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-76ww="true">carousel advertising</a></li><li><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/interactive+advertising" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-r2eq="true">interactive advertising</a></li><li><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/eye-tracking" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-gfm5="true">eye-tracking</a></li><li><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/consumer+attention" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-g4pd="true">consumer attention</a></li><li><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/brand+recall" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-ebbh="true">brand recall</a></li><li><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/keyword/perceived+control" class="kwd-btn keyword-click" kameleoonlistener-50r1="true">perceived control</a></li></ul></div></div></div><div id="embedded-pdf-target" class="with-border"></div><div class="pb-dropzone" data-pb-dropzone="contentNavigationDropZoneAbs"><div class="widget gql-content-navigation none  widget-none" id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e">

            <div class="widget-body body body-none "><div class="ajaxWidget loading" data-ajax-widget="gql-content-navigation" data-ajax-widget-id="2ffb43c7-15dc-4c79-9e29-8e4bed9b3d1e" data-ajax-observe="true"></div></div>
        </div>
    </div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0001"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e144">Introduction</h2><p>For advertising to be effective, it must capture consumers’ attention. In busy, cluttered social media environments, advertisements constantly compete for consumers’ attention (Duff and Segijn <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0015" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>), such that attention becomes an exceptionally limited resource (Bergkvist and Langner <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0003" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>; Beuckels et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0005" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>; Nelson-Field, Riebe, and Sharp <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0044" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2013</a></span>). For example, Instagram users look at ads for only 1.6 s on average (Borgmann, Kopka, and Langner <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0008" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>), and more than 80% of ads fail to spark at least 2.5 s of attention, as is needed for lasting brand impact (WARC <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0068" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). Thus, identifying ad formats that can better attract and maintain consumers’ attention represents a critical consideration for advertisers and researchers.</p><p>Among various formats available in social media newsfeeds, carousel ads have emerged as a unique version of in-feed advertising, available on most platforms, including Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, and LinkedIn (<a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0001" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0001" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0001" data-registered="">Appendix 1</a>). Unlike static images or auto-play videos, which conform to habitual, vertical scrolling behavior, carousel ads require users to perform a deliberate, sideways swipe to explore additional brand content (Wei et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0069" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>). The directional shift introduces a unique consumer interaction that may foster higher perceived control. This psychological mechanism in turn can influence attention and memory and, thus, ad effectiveness. In addition, the multi-card structure of carousel ads supports storytelling, which could enhance users’ immersion and processing. By breaking the marketing information into smaller, more navigable units, carousel ads might improve consumers’ comprehension and sense of connection with the message (Oltra, Camarero, and San José Cabezudo <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0045" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). These effects underscore the importance of examining carousel ads as a distinct, promising tactic for capturing attention and enhancing brand recall.</p><p>Despite their growing prevalence and anecdotal reports of their success, carousel ads have prompted limited scholarly attention. Industry reports suggest that carousel ads produce better performance metrics, such as clickthrough rates, than other sponsored posts (Sloane <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0060" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>). But among scholarly studies dedicated to advertising effectiveness (e.g. Huang et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0028" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Jung and Im <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0032" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>; Liu-Thompkins <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0039" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>), carousel ads have been largely neglected thus far (De Keyzer, Dens, and De Pelsmacker <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0013" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>), with a few exceptions of studies with student samples that identify strong engagement outcomes (Wahid and Gunarto <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0066" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>) and more effective calls-to-action (Oltra, Camarero, and San José Cabezudo <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0045" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). However, the broader implications of carousel ads for advertising effectiveness, defined here as attention and brand recall, remain unknown. We also lack sufficient insights into what drives consumers to engage with this format in the first place, which represents a critical consideration, given its opt-in nature. In response, we propose the notion of a <i>carousel effect</i>, defined as a user-driven interaction with carousel ads that enhances attention and brand recall. We propose further that this effect is fueled by two related mechanisms: perceived control, stemming from consumers’ ability to self-direct the interaction, and narrative transportation, which results from sequential storytelling enabled by multi-card formats.</p><p>In addition to addressing a timely research gap, we seek a methodological contribution. That is, attention research frequently relies on laboratory studies (e.g. Cummins, Gong, and Reichert <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0011" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>; Smit, Boerman, and van Meurs <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0061" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>), but we aim to understand consumers’ attention to carousel ads in the real world. Thus, we combine qualitative interviews, eye-tracking, and videography studies; participants use their own smartphones and view their own social media newsfeeds. In an initial, qualitative study, we explore consumers’ perceptions of and experiences with carousel ads relative to other in-feed advertising formats. With this multimethod approach, we can address a central research question: <i>How do consumers evaluate and experience carousel ads compared with other in-feed ad formats in social media?</i></p><p class="last">In turn, we make several contributions to advertising and social media literature. First, we conceptualize the proposed <i>carousel effect</i> as a distinct form of ad engagement, driven by the combination of user-initiated interactions and a multi-card message structure. This concept extends existing advertising response models by foregrounding the role of opt-in behaviors and self-directed content navigation—features that are highly relevant in mobile and social media contexts. Second, we depict a four-stage experiential process of carousel ad engagement, which provides a structured account of how consumers interact with multi-card formats and also deepens theory related to ad-induced narrative transportation and attention. Third, our findings show that activated carousels elicit significantly more attention, thereby underscoring the persuasive potential of perceived control and narrative storytelling in shaping ad effectiveness. Fourth, we extend the attitude–behavior consistency framework to mobile advertising domains by demonstrating the impact of strong brands on carousel activation. In support of these contributions, we begin the next section by developing our theoretical framework around perceived control and narrative transportation.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0002"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e220">Theoretical framework and hypotheses development</h2><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0002-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e222">Carousel ads in social media</h3><p class="last">Infinite-scroll newsfeeds represent the default navigation design on most social media platforms (Echauri <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0016" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>). Designed to be endless, such feeds continuously display relevant content to consumers, in an effort to maximize their engagement (Facebook <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0017" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2018</a></span>). This constant content flow can readily induce information overload, so attracting consumer attention becomes increasingly difficult (Borgmann, Kopka, and Langner <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0008" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). Advertisers can choose among four different ad formats: (1) <i>image ads</i> that feature a single still image; (2) <i>video ads</i> that display moving picture content; (3) <i>carousel ads</i>, consisting of at least two swipeable cards; and (4) <i>collection ads</i>, which present a main image with smaller images below. Unlike static or autoplay formats that reinforce natural, upward scrolling behavior, carousel ads require a sideways swipe that interrupts the default feed behavior. This opt-in interaction introduces user agency and control: Consumers must make a decision to activate the ad by swiping, and once it is activated, they can control the direction and pace of the interaction. This unique, opt-in, self-directed format raises new questions about how its distinctive interactivity, perceived control, and narrative structure might affect attention and brand memory.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0002-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e248">Interactivity that provides perceived control</h3><p>The first card of a carousel ad is the only one shown by default; consumers must intentionally swipe sideways to explore more. This structure introduces a form of interactivity that enables users to control and modify their message exposure (Liu and Shrum <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2002</a></span>; Steuer <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0062" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1992</a></span>). Once they engage with a carousel post, consumers determine the pacing, sequencing, and depth of interaction, by swiping forward or back, skipping, or lingering. Unlike traditional linear storytelling, user-directed stories allow the audience to influence the narrative’s progression, structure, or outcome through their choices or interactions. For example, in the carousel ad in <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0001" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 1</button>, a consumer might swipe back to the first or second card to see the car in greater detail. These interactive narratives offer multiple paths or options, giving users a sense of agency and control, which can increase enjoyment, identification, and engagement (Dillman Carpentier, Rogers, and Barnard <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0014" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>; Green and Brock <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0021" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2000</a></span>; Green and Jenkins <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0022" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>). In psychology, perceived control refers to a person’s beliefs in their ability to influence their environment (Skinner <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0059" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1996</a></span>); in marketing, it is associated with greater satisfaction and increased engagement (Hui and Bateson <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0029" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1991</a></span>; Hu and Wise <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0027" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). The participants in Wei et al. (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0069" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>) investigation of carousel ads accordingly report greater perceived control, associated positively with message engagement. Similar to skippable video ads (Frade, de Oliveira, and Giraldi <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0020" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>), opt-in carousel interactions might reduce irritation and enhance satisfaction by allowing users to direct the progression of the content themselves. Formats that support such user control tend to foster deeper involvement (Dillman Carpentier, Rogers, and Barnard <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0014" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>; Hameed and Perkis <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0025" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2018</a></span>).</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 1. </span></span> Example carousel ad with five cards.</p><p class="captionText">Source: We created these images using ChatGPT-4o and DALL-E (2025).</p></div><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0001" data-registered=""><img id="d1e300" src="https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/4e891d04-12b7-4633-86ca-a3c2dc43a9e8/rina_a_2624918_f0001_c.jpg" loading="lazy" height="197" width="500" alt="Figure 1. Example carousel ad with five cards.Source: We created these images using ChatGPT-4o and DALL-E (2025)." class="figure-image"></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0001" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Display full size</button></div></div></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0003"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e303">Multi-card structure supports narrative transportation</h2><p>The carousel format also supports storytelling, because the content unfolds card-by-card. Rather than displaying all the information at once, carousel ads present only a portion of the content initially, then invite consumers to uncover more by swiping sideways. This unfolding format can stimulate curiosity, similar to mystery appeals in entertainment media (Knobloch-Westerwick and Keplinger <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0034" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2006</a></span>). The multi-card structure also signals narrative flow because the swipeable sequence presents a beginning, middle, and end of a story. For example, in <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0001" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 1</button>, a young man takes the advertised car into an adventurous mountain terrain, then does some hiking, and finally enjoys a campfire with a friend. Such an unfolding structure can support narrative transportation (Green and Brock <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0021" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2000</a></span>), such that consumers become mentally and emotionally immersed in the story. As they swipe through the carousel, they experience the brand content at their self-determined, chosen pace, which allows for longer attention that in turn tends to enhance brand memory. The vivid imagery and emotional communication thus provided help strengthen narrative transportation, which then might lead to enhanced persuasion (Van Laer et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0065" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>).</p><p>Narrative transportation theory provides a foundation for understanding user-driven immersion in interactive storytelling and advertising. It describes a deep cognitive and emotional engagement with story elements and anticipation of what comes next (Phillips and McQuarrie <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0047" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>; Thomas and Grigsby <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0063" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>). In a study conducted on Instagram, Lim and Childs (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0037" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>) find that story- versus product-focused posts prompt participants to report stronger narrative transportation, such as imagining themselves within a scene. That is, narrative transportation can foster immersion, a state characterized by heightened attention (e.g. longer gaze duration), and affective engagement (Van Laer et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0065" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>; Wang, Gohary, and Chan <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0067" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>).</p><p>Because carousel ads combine perceived control and narrative transportation, they might instill a <i>carousel effect</i>, which we define as a user-driven, immersive experience that can draw greater attention to the brand than static formats and that also should lead to increased memory encoding (MacInnis and Jaworski <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0040" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1989</a></span>; Rossiter, Percy, and Bergkvist <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0056" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2018</a></span>; Wilson, Baack, and Till <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0070" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2015</a></span>). With the recognition that attention and memory encoding are key predictors of brand recall (Guitart, Hervet, and Hildebrand <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0024" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>; Simmonds et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>), we hypothesize:
</p><p id="mthst1"></p><p class="first last">H1: Activated carousel ads elicit (a) longer gaze durations, (b) more fixations, and (c) better brand recall than other ad formats.</p><p></p><p></p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0003-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e359">Impacts of carousel length on interaction and attention</h3><p class="last">Carousel ads vary in length, measured by the number of cards they include. At a minimum, they feature two cards; their length is visually indicated by navigation dots beneath the images. Consumers move through the cards one at a time and may disengage at any point. Most feature three to five cards, though some platforms allow up to twenty (e.g. Instagram, <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0001" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0001" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0001" data-registered="">Appendix 1</a>). Longer carousel ads naturally provide more interaction opportunities and greater potential for sustaining attention. Research involving smartphone interactions suggests that swiping-based environments encourage prolonged engagement, as when Heitmayer and Lahlou (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0026" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>) show that apps with swiping-based newsfeeds sustain longer interactions, because users fall into a continuous loop motion (Rixen et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0053" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>). Lahlou (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0036" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>) characterizes this type of interaction as a “cognitive attractor,” because it offers small, satisfying interactions, with low effort and high stimulus salience, that effectively anchor attention. Because they offer more content and opportunities for interaction, longer carousel ads should increase the likelihood of continued viewing and thus capture more attention:
</p><p id="mthst2"></p><p class="first last">H2: The more cards an activated carousel ad contains, the (a) longer the gaze duration and (b) higher the number of fixations.</p><p></p><p></p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0003-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e377">Impacts of brand attitude on carousel activation</h3><p>Due to their opt-in feature, carousel ads require an active behavioral decision: Consumers must choose to swipe through the ad to engage with its full content. We predict their decision to do so reflects their attitudes toward the brand. The attitude–behavior consistency framework (Fazio and Zanna <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0018" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1981</a></span>; Kraus <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0035" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1995</a></span>) explicitly indicates that people engage in behaviors that align with their existing attitudes. If consumers evaluate a brand favorably, they exhibit more positive behaviors, such as involvement, engagement, or positive word of mouth. Prior research consistently links brand attitudes to behaviors, such as increased attention or choice (Gresham and Shimp <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0023" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1985</a></span>). In their eye-tracking study, Bialkova, Grunert, and van Trijp (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0006" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>) determine that brand attitude powerfully drives both attention to and choices of products on supermarket shelves. Positive brand evaluations also guide people’s visual attention, particularly in the presence of competing stimuli (Roskos-Ewoldsen and Fazio <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0055" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1992</a></span>). That is, consumers tend to interact more with strong brands, particularly when their engagement is voluntary, as when they choose whether to swipe an ad.</p><p class="last">In social media contexts specifically, stronger brand attitudes have been linked to increased engagement with branded posts, including more likes, comments, and shares (Rietveld et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0052" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). Thus, strong brands should attract both attention and active engagement, particularly in newsfeed-based environments, where carousel ads appear alongside other content. Building on this logic, we propose that carousel ads featuring strong brands are more likely to be swiped.
</p><p id="mthst3"></p><p class="first last">H3: Better attitudes toward advertised brands increase the likelihood that carousel ads are activated.</p><p></p><p></p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0003-S2003"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e403">Overview of studies</h3><p class="last">To test these predictions, we conduct four studies, with diverse methods. By exploring consumers’ perceptions of carousel ads in Study 1, we identify four experiential themes—curiosity, convenience, perceived control, and immersion—that help define the carousel effect. We test for the effect empirically in Study 2, using mobile eye-tracking to measure attention and brand recall across advertising formats. With an online experiment (Study 3a) and mobile videography field study (Study 3b), we then examine the effects of brand attitudes on carousel activation. In the General Discussion section, <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="t0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table" data-registered="">Table 2</button> summarizes the findings of these four multimethod studies.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0004"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e410">Study 1: qualitative assessments of consumers’ perceptions of carousel ads</h2><p>With this exploratory, qualitative investigation, we explore how consumers perceive and evaluate carousel ads compared with other in-feed advertising formats. Our goal is to establish consumers’ awareness of various ad formats and discern how they experience and interpret the unique interactive features of carousel ads during their actual social media usage. The findings thus reveal consumers’ awareness, attitudes, and behaviors toward carousel ads.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0004-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e413">Method</h3><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0004-S2001-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e415">Participants and study design</h4><p class="last">We conducted qualitative interviews with 22 participants (59% women, <i>M</i><sub>age</sub> = 29.0 years, <i>SD</i><sub>age</sub> = 12.4), whom we identified with a convenience sampling approach, in which we deliberately sought non-student informants. They are diverse in age (20 to 72 years) and include both working adults (64%) and university students (36%). All interviews took place in participants’ homes between May and August 2024 and lasted 20–40 min. We screened the participants to ensure they were regular Instagram or Facebook users, so we could reasonably capture their general awareness of different in-feed ad formats and their perceptions of and behaviors related to carousel ads in real-world settings. Facebook and Instagram represent the most popular global sites, measured in terms of newsfeed usage and number of monthly active users (i.e. 3 billion Facebook and 2 billion Instagram monthly active users; DataReportal <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0012" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0004-S2001-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e430">Procedure and data analysis</h4><p>The semi-structured interview guide included probing ad examples, such that we asked participants to evaluate the ad format rather than any specific content, which we explicitly presented as a reference only. The examples, gathered from Instagram and Facebook, represent four available in-feed ad formats (image, video, carousel, collection; see <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0002" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0002" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0002" data-registered="">Appendix 2</a>); we selected them for their visual clarity, neutrality, and reference to typical platform use. All participants saw the same examples, then indicated how often they had come across and interacted with each format (“not at all” = 0, “very often” = 6). Next, we raised three open-ended questions: “What do you think about this ad format?” “What bothers you about this advertising format?” and “What do you like about this advertising format?” In total, we conducted more than 9 h of qualitative interviews, transcribed using GoSpeech AI-transcription software.</p><p>The thematic analysis of these transcripts followed a structured process (Naeem et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0043" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>). After familiarizing ourselves with the transcripts, we coded key segments in MAXQDA in accordance with the interview guide. Emerging patterns were grouped into corresponding themes and refined iteratively through cross-case comparisons to capture common descriptions of participants’ awareness, attitudes, and experiences with each ad format. This process revealed four overarching themes that structure consumers’ experiences with carousel ads, which we conceptualized as curiosity, convenience, self-control, and immersion stages. In addition, we conducted an idiosyncratic analysis to explore how participants described the sequence of their experiences. It revealed a consistent order across cases, in support of an interpretation of these themes as progressive stages. In depicting this sequence, <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 2</button> illustrates a typical flow of consumers’ engagement with carousel ads.</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 2. </span></span> Stages of carousel ad experiences.</p></div><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0002" data-registered=""><img id="d1e451" src="https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/47a544ff-f2ce-4e9d-9515-e1c100038845/rina_a_2624918_f0002_c.jpg" loading="lazy" height="107" width="500" alt="Figure 2. Stages of carousel ad experiences." class="figure-image"></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0002" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Display full size</button></div></div></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0004-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e454">Results</h3><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0004-S2002-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e456">Evaluation of carousel ads</h4><p>Participants indicated frequent exposures to and interactions with all four in-feed ad formats. In terms of favorability, they frequently expressed preferences for the carousel ad format, due to its less intrusive nature and greater information provision, as well as their ability to control it (<button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="t0001" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table" data-registered="">Table 1</button>).</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 1. </span> Example ad format evaluations.</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="t0001-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0001&doi=10.1080%2F02650487.2026.2624918&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="t0001" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table" data-registered="">Display Table</a></div></div><p class="last">When describing <i>image ads</i>, participants praised their simplicity but found them annoying, due to frequent exposures and unrelated content. <i>Video ads</i> evoked similar assessments; participants also mentioned skipping this format most quickly. Even if video ads provide more information, their linear, fixed viewing conditions and sudden interruptions by sound are unpopular. One participant cited the information provided by the multiple images in <i>collection ads</i>, but most participants found that format confusing. In turn, to understand why participants consistently expressed preferences for carousel ads and define what sets them apart, we conducted a deeper, two-step exploration of how consumers experience these ads, using both idiosyncratic and cross-case analyses (Fournier <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0019" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1998</a></span>; Rahman, Langner, and Temme <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0050" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0004-S2002-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e554">Idiosyncratic analysis</h4><p>Participants described their interactions with carousel ads in stages, starting with curiosity, moving through convenience and self-control, and resulting in immersion, as illustrated in <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 2</button>.</p><p>For example, Participant 1 (P1, male, age 22) described the appeal created by the first card, noting “it happens when the first image appeals to me,” which triggered his <i>curiosity</i> and “then you want more information.” He preferred swiping over clicking too, which he finds more <i>convenient</i>: “Instead of clicking on it, you have the option to swipe … [so] the threshold for interaction is definitely lower.” Another convenience benefit emerges because he does not have to leave the platform (e.g. Instagram) or “go to an external page to get more information and see even more.” By lowering this participant’s interaction barriers, these features increase the likelihood of an interaction.</p><p class="last">Similarly, P8 (male, age 27) describes how, at the start of the interaction process, “out of curiosity, I tend to swipe to the side,” and also praises the convenience of the format, because “they are not distracting” and “I rather tend to swipe to the side” (cf. clicking). Once the carousel begins, P8 also notes the appeal of <i>self-control</i>, such that he can swipe at his own pace, and greater <i>immersion</i> with the ad content, achieved through intense content consumption, in that “I interact with [carousel ads] the most and spend more time with the content.”</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0004-S2002-S3003"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e577">Cross-case analysis</h4><p>Combining the data across participants reveals some deeper insights into the four stages of the carousel ad experience. Overall, <i>curiosity</i> emerges as the main initiator of carousel ad activation. The first image in a carousel ad serves as the entry point to a sequence of cards, and users feel motivated by a desire to see what follows. This element of curiosity, combined with the potential for surprise, is distinctive to the carousel format:
</p><div class="quote"><p class="first">… you can already see a bit of the next thing coming. And when you see the first image, you think maybe there’s more. (P12, male, age 41)</p><p class="last">I think if you’re interested in the topic, then it’s always exciting to see what’s on the next page. Because that’s a bit of a surprise, so to speak. (P4, female, age 17)</p></div>
The <i>convenience</i> of sideways swiping then accelerates the interaction with carousel ads. Consumers, well-acquainted with swiping navigation, find this interaction less inhibiting than actions like clicking a call-to-action button. Through sideways swiping, users can engage with the ad without leaving the social media feed and maintain a seamless experience within the same media environment. Once users begin swiping through a carousel, they appreciate the ease of comparing different elements, which can also add to their enjoyment:
<div class="quote"><p class="first">You get a good overview if you are interested and that you can swipe through the ad again and do not need to leave the page. I don’t click on links or on the button for shopping, but I swipe carousels. (P6, male, age 31)</p><p class="last">It’s more fun to swipe left and right and then always have one product in focus and decide whether it’s cool or not. (P7, male, age 25)</p></div>
Such convenience aligns with the <i>self-control</i> users maintain, based on their ability to decide whether to engage with the ad and their freedom to manage the speed and direction of interaction once they have swiped. In addition to navigating through the content at their own pace, users can choose how much detail to explore, which enhances the overall interaction experience:
<div class="quote"><p class="first">You can then decide for yourself how long you want to stay on a page or a photo from this carousel or to swipe away. (P4, female, age 17)</p><p class="last">I think it’s good that you can click through as quickly as possible … so the speed at which you want to click through is up to you…. With video it goes on and on, of course you can stop it, but it’s more complicated. And here you can swipe or stop within seconds. (P14, female, age 22)</p></div>
Finally, participants report a greater sense of <i>immersion</i> when engaging with carousel ads, such that they become involved with the content. They even lose track of how many cards they have viewed or swiped through before reaching the last card. Through this deeper interaction, they absorb more information, gain a better understanding, and learn more about the advertised content:<p></p><div class="quote"><p class="first">I’ve already caught myself looking at 10–20 things. You’re more curious and spend more time intensely looking at it. (P12, male, age 41)</p><p>You get more insight into the product, from the features or images presented, than if you only have a single picture or a video. You can see the variety better. (P4, female, age 17)</p><p class="last">Whether it’s a product or a travel trip, you can then swipe through, take a look at it at your leisure … and you can now learn more than just in one picture. (P20, female, age 27)</p></div></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0004-S2003"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e610">Discussion</h3><p class="last">The Study 1 participants report familiarity with various in-feed ad formats but also express a clear a preference for carousel ads, citing their less intrusive nature and ease of interaction. Our qualitative analysis reveals four key stages of consumer interactions with carousel ads: (1) curiosity, (2) convenience, (3) perceived control, and (4) immersion. Initially, the carousel ad must spark curiosity to prompt user activation. Sideways swiping, which is a familiar, low-effort action for the participants, seems more convenient than actions that require them to exit the feed. Moreover, carousel ads grant consumers a greater sense of control over when to activate the ad and the speed and direction of content consumption, in line with findings that indicate that users’ control reduces perceived intrusiveness (Frade, de Oliveira, and Giraldi <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0020" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>). Finally, participants report more profound engagement with and absorption in the content, indicating increased immersion (Phillips and McQuarrie <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0047" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>; Van Laer et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0065" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>).</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0005"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e623">Study 2: eye-tracking experiment to measure attention</h2><p>Building on these insights, in Study 2 we empirically test whether activating carousel ads leads to increased visual attention and brand recall during real-world social media usage. To analyze how much attention consumers devote to carousel ads versus other in-feed ad formats, we gathered eye-tracking data from participants, using their own devices in real-life viewing conditions (Read et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0051" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>). These data were obtained from a previous study, designed to understand typical smartphone swiping behavior (Rohrbach et al., <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT6635437" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>).<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref en"><a data-rid="EN0001" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="fn" data-label="footnote" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Footnote</span><sup>1</sup></a></span></p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0005-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e635">Method</h3><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0005-S2001-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e637">Participants and study design</h4><p>Thirty-six participants (21 to 58 years; 61% women; <i>M</i><sub>age</sub> = 30.5 years, <i>SD</i><sub>age</sub> = 9.4) took part in the study. Because mobile eye-tracking studies in dynamic environments demand substantial resources to support the individual setups and manual coding of areas of interest (AOI), their sample sizes usually range around 30 participants (Meißner et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0041" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>; Pfeiffer et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0046" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>); the Study 2 sample aligns with these standards. To gather robust, real-world insights, we recruited regular Instagram users, according to a convenience sampling approach, who reported average daily usage of 1.24 h (<i>SD</i> = .95). We deliberately sought a heterogeneous sample; it comprised 81% employed adults and 19% university students, across various professional backgrounds. The data collection took place in participants’ homes at different times of day. We chose Instagram as the study platform because, in terms of user engagement, it attracts the most time spent per user (1 h and 10 min) and the most daily sessions (11.8) (DataReportal <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0012" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>).</p><p class="last">To assess attention, we used two standard eye-tracking metrics: gaze duration in milliseconds (ms) and number of fixations. Gaze duration captures the total time spent viewing the ad; fixations reflect the number of times the viewer’s gaze paused on the ad content, as the AOI. For brand recall, we asked participants to freely recall any brand they saw during their previous Instagram session. Only accurate, unaided recalls that matched the recorded ad exposures, verified through ego-perspective eye-tracking video data, were considered valid.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0005-S2001-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e663">Procedure and data analysis</h4><p>Each participant was briefed, using a structured interview guide, and equipped with a mobile eye-tracking device (Tobii Pro Glasses 2; see <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0003" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 3</button>) that recorded their field of vision, fixations, and gaze duration using infrared corneal reflection technology. These devices are capable of precise tracking of attention in real-world environments, including mobile Instagram browsing.</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 3. </span></span> Experimental setup, Study 2.</p></div><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0003" data-registered=""><img id="d1e676" src="https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/da25b7d2-bad8-4586-9a74-04e07f392fcc/rina_a_2624918_f0003_c.jpg" loading="lazy" height="237" width="500" alt="Figure 3. Experimental setup, Study 2." class="figure-image"></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0003" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Display full size</button></div></div><p class="last">We asked the participants to browse their Instagram newsfeeds as they normally would for at least 2 min, to ensure sufficient data collection. After each session, they provided their unaided brand recall, and the eye-tracking data were exported into iMotions 9.3. The AOI for all sponsored posts (<i>n</i> = 435) were coded frame-by-frame, to reflect the dynamic nature of mobile eye-tracking. A sponsored post would be logged as viewable from the moment that 50% of it appeared on screen until 50% of it had exited (Trabulsi et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0064" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>). We set the minimum duration for a fixation at 80 ms, which is the generally accepted sufficient duration to allow cognitive processing of stimuli, as established in previous mobile attention studies (Boerman and Müller <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0007" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>).</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0005-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e690">Results</h3><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0005-S2002-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e692">Attention and brand recall</h4><p>To analyze H1, in which we predicted that activated carousel ads draw more attention than image, video, or collection ads, we ran generalized linear mixed effects models. For gaze duration, we used a Gamma distribution with a log-link (Rosbergen, Pieters, and Wedel <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0054" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1997</a></span>). Fixation frequency is a count variable, so for that variable, we used a Poisson distribution with a log-link (Pieters, Warlop, and Wedel <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0048" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2002</a></span>). The brand recall measure reflects a generalized linear mixed effects model with a binomial distribution and a logit link (Simmonds et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0058" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). We also included random intercepts to account for variation in the outcome variable, attributable to each participant (Barr <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0002" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2013</a></span>; Judd, Westfall, and Kenny <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0031" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>; Quené and van den Bergh <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0049" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>).</p><p>According to planned contrasts with a Bonferroni correction, activated carousel ads (<i>M</i> = 7,799 ms) are attended to significantly longer than image ads (<i>M</i> = 1,276 ms, <i>p</i> < .001), video ads (<i>M</i> = 1,512 ms, <i>p</i> < .001), collection ads (<i>M</i> = 1,363 ms, <i>p</i> < .001), and non-activated carousel ads (<i>M</i> = 1,370 ms, <i>p</i> < .001). They also prompt more frequent fixations (<i>M</i> = 19.250) than image ads (<i>M</i> = 3.795, <i>p</i> < .001), video ads (<i>M</i> = 4.215, <i>p</i> < .001), collection ads (<i>M</i> = 3.333, <i>p</i> < .001), or non-activated carousel ads (<i>M</i> = 3.732, <i>p</i> < .001). Furthermore, participants recalled the activated carousel ads significantly better (<i>M</i> = .458) than image ads (<i>M</i> = .031, <i>p</i> < .01), video ads (<i>M</i> = .038, <i>p</i> < .01), collection ads (<i>M</i> = .111, <i>p</i> < .01), or non-activated carousel ads (<i>M</i> = .080, <i>p</i> < .01). These findings, which we summarize in <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0004" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 4</button>, offer support for H1a–H1c.</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 4. </span></span> Mean gaze duration, number of fixations, and brand recall by ad format.</p><p class="captionText">Notes: CA = carousel ad.</p></div><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0004" data-registered=""><img id="d1e812" src="https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/f75db5cc-2fed-4b06-bd50-eba2bb8bae52/rina_a_2624918_f0004_c.jpg" loading="lazy" height="258" width="500" alt="Figure 4. Mean gaze duration, number of fixations, and brand recall by ad format.Notes: CA = carousel ad." class="figure-image"></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0004" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Display full size</button></div></div><p class="last">The observed carousel effect is strong. Across all ad exposures (i.e. activated and non-activated), carousel ads (<i>M</i> = 2,760 ms) are attended to significantly longer than image ads (<i>M</i> = 1,276 ms, <i>p</i> < .001), video ads (<i>M</i> = 1,512 ms, <i>p</i> < .014), and collection ads (<i>M</i> = 1,363 ms, <i>p</i> < .019). They also attract more fixations (<i>M</i> = 7.245) than image ads (<i>M</i> = 3.795, <i>p</i> < .001), video ads (<i>M</i> = 4.215, <i>p</i> < .001), and collection ads (<i>M</i> = 3.333, <i>p</i> < .036). Finally, carousel ads are recalled significantly better (<i>M</i> = .162) than image ads (<i>M</i> = .031, <i>p</i> < .01) and video ads (<i>M</i> = .038, <i>p</i> < .01), though not better than collection ads (<i>M</i> = .111, <i>p</i> = .47).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0005-S2002-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e883">Effects of longer carousel ads on attention</h4><p class="last">To investigate whether longer carousel ads increase attention to the ad, we conducted generalized linear regressions, again using a Gamma distribution with a log-link for gaze duration and a Poisson distribution with a log-link for the number of fixations. The results indicate significant effects of the number of cards on gaze duration (<i>b</i> = .084, <i>p</i> < .001) and number of fixations (<i>b</i> = .064, <i>p</i> < .001). In other words, carousel ads with more cards resulted in longer viewing times and more fixations, in support of H2.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0005-S2003"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e899">Discussion</h3><p>These analyses of consumers’ attention to carousel ads and recall of advertised brands reveal that carousel ads in general attract significantly more attention than image, video, or collections ads. Attention to any ad is limited; we find an overall total average of 1.4 s, consistent with prior research dealing with social media attention (Borgmann, Kopka, and Langner <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0008" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>). But as our findings clarify, the activated carousel ads strongly increase attention, as well as brand recall (by a factor of five), in support of H1. Non-activated carousel ads produce results similar to those of other in-feed ad formats in terms of attention and brand recall. Therefore, advertisers can benefit from carousel formats—but only if consumers activate them.</p><p class="last">Attention to carousel ads also increases when they include more cards, as we predicted in H2. Notably, participants in Study 2 consistently swiped through the activated carousel ads to the final available card. This result arguably might reflect a desirable social behavior, evoked by the presence of the eye-tracking device, but we find this alternative explanation generally unconvincing. The observed behavior in Study 2 closely mirrors the self-reported behavior from Study 1, in which participants continuously reported swiping to the last card as a natural, habitual response to activated carousel ads, driven by curiosity or interest. Even if interest in a carousel ad ultimately might decline beyond some extreme length, behavioral fatigue appears unlikely within existing platform constraints (e.g. Instagram’s 20-card limit; Sato <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0057" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>). The technical restrictions seemingly prevent the potential onset of diminishing attention.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0006"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e911">Study 3: brand effects on carousel activation</h2><p>To test for effects of brand attitudes on the decision to initiate sideways swiping behaviors on carousel ads, we designed an online, scenario-like experiment, in which we asked participants how likely they were to swipe into a carousel ad. Then with a videography study, we measure consumers’ real-world behaviors toward carousel ads and establish more robust support for the findings.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0006-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e914">Study 3a: online experiment</h3><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2001-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e916">Participants and study design</h4><p class="last">For this online experiment, we collected a student sample from two public universities and a non-student sample from Prolific. A total of 96 students (74% women, <i>M</i><sub>age</sub> = 22.7 years, <i>SD</i><sub>age</sub> = 3.1) were interviewed. To increase the external validity of our study, we also collected a non-student sample of 37 participants from Prolific (27% women, <i>M</i><sub>age</sub> = 33.2 years, <i>SD</i><sub>age</sub> = 9.6). Having found no differences between samples in the means of the dependent variables, we combined them for the analysis. As a manipulation check, we asked participants if they were familiar with carousel ads; in support of this check, we provided them with a visual example and short explanation of carousel posts (i.e. they can be swiped sideways to reveal multiple images and are commonly found in the newsfeeds of platforms like Instagram or Facebook; <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0003" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0003" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0003" data-registered="">Appendix 3</a>). Accordingly, our focus was on a general carousel format, rather than any platform-specific execution. We excluded 11 participants who failed the manipulation check or provided incomplete responses, leaving a final sample of 122 respondents (60% women, <i>M</i><sub>age</sub> = 25.9 years, <i>SD</i><sub>age</sub> = 7.6).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2001-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e948">Procedure and data analysis</h4><p class="last">To identify strong brands (Keller <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0033" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1993</a></span>) from six product categories, we relied on Interbrand (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0030" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2023</a></span>) ratings. Then we included weak brands not listed by Interbrand but that compete in the same category as the selected strong brands and have international reach (<a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0004" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0004" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0004" data-registered="">Appendix 4</a>). The online survey started by asking participants to indicate the likelihood that they would swipe into a carousel ad from given brand (“not at all” = 0, “very likely” = 6; <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0005" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0005" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0005" data-registered="">Appendix 5</a>). To establish a combined between- and within-subject design, each participant was assigned randomly to see strong or weak brands. As a manipulation check, we asked participants to indicate their attitudes toward the randomly assigned brands (“bad” = −3, “good” = +3; <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#APP0006" data-behaviour="scroll" data-behaviour-ref="#APP0006" data-behaviour-callback="focus" data-behaviour-callback-target="#APP0006" data-registered="">Appendix 6</a>) according to Bergkvist and Rossiter (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0004" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2001-S3003"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e971">Results</h4><p>With a linear mixed model, we check whether participants’ brand attitudes were better for the strong versus weak brands; the planned contrasts affirm that attitudes toward strong brands were better (<i>M</i><sub>strong</sub> = 1.399; <i>M</i><sub>weak</sub> = .198, <i>p</i> < .001). We compared both strong and weak brands in each product category separately too, and in each category, participants’ attitudes remained better for the strong than the weak brands (all <i>p</i> < .001). This manipulation check confirms our selection of strong and weak brands.</p><p>To test for the likelihood that they activate carousel ads for strong versus weak brands, we ran another linear mixed model with random intercepts for participants (Barr <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0002" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2013</a></span>; Judd, Westfall, and Kenny <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0031" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2012</a></span>; Quené and van den Bergh <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0049" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2008</a></span>). The planned contrasts reveal a greater likelihood of swiping on strong brands (<i>M</i> = 3.542) than on weak brands (<i>M</i> = 1.917, <i>p</i> < .001; <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="F0005" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Figure 5</button>), in support of H3.</p><div class="figureView"><div class="short-legend"><p class="captionText"><span aria-level="3" role="heading"><span class="captionLabel">Figure 5. </span></span> Mean likelihood of carousel activation, strong versus weak brands.</p></div><a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" class="thumbnail" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-id="F0005" data-registered=""><img id="d1e1019" src="https://www.tandfonline.com/cms/asset/7ac1dfae-613a-4e34-ab38-56c96e06bf72/rina_a_2624918_f0005_c.jpg" loading="lazy" height="500" width="434" alt="Figure 5. Mean likelihood of carousel activation, strong versus weak brands." class="figure-image"></a><div><button class="show-full-size btn btn-sm" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-id="F0005" data-popup-event-type="fig" data-registered="">Display full size</button></div></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2001-S3004"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e1022">Discussion</h4><p class="last">These experimental findings indicate that carousel ads posted by strong brands are 1.8 times more likely to be activated than those featuring weak brands. This finding reflects participants’ behavioral intentions, not their actual behavior, so to establish the validity of this result, we also conducted a field study and use videography to observe actual behavior in real-world contexts.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0006-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e1025">Study 3b: videography study</h3><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2002-S3001"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e1027">Participants and study design</h4><p class="last">Sixty-nine participants took part in this study (38% women; age range 15–55 years, <i>M</i><sub>age</sub> = 26.1 years, <i>SD</i><sub>age</sub> = 9.3), of whom 57% were employed and 43% were students. All participants were active Instagram users, averaging 1.3 h of daily usage. We rely on Instagram specifically for Study 3b, due to its dominance in terms of user engagement (DataReportal <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0012" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>); participants likely were familiar with its carousel format. The experiment took place in participants’ homes, at different times of the day.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2002-S3002"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e1042">Procedure and data analysis</h4><p class="last">The participants were equipped with mobile-eye tracking glasses (Tobii Pro 2), which we used to record their media consumption, from their point of view. The instructions asked them to use their own Instagram newsfeeds as they normally would. A trained research assistant also monitored the content on each participant’s smartphone and logged all carousel ads. After each session, participants were shown the carousel ads again, as logged by iMotions 9.3, and asked about their interaction behavior using open-ended questions such as, “Why did you swipe sideways into this carousel ad?” In addition, participants rated their attitudes toward the brand featured in each logged carousel ad, from “bad” (−3) to “good” (+3) (Bergkvist and Rossiter <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0004" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2007</a></span>), whether those ads were activated or not.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2002-S3003"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e1049">Results</h4><p class="last">Attitude toward the brand emerges as a critical determinant of carousel activation. The participants’ positive past experiences with the brand or favorable evaluations of it influenced their decision to engage further:
</p><div class="quote"><p class="first">This was a great post, and I love the brand. (P2, female, age 24)</p><p class="last">This is a well-known brand, so I trusted it and swiped to explore more. (P22, male, age 30)</p></div>
Favorable brand attitudes also seem to support further interactions. According to a logistic regression, the significant effect of attitude toward the brand on carousel ad activation (<i>b</i> = .432, <i>p</i> < .001) indicates that the better the attitude, the higher the chance of carousel ad activation, in support of H3.<p></p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_3" id="S0006-S2002-S3004"><h4 class="section-heading-4" id="d1e1063">Discussion</h4><p class="last">Positive attitudes toward a brand increase the likelihood that a consumer activates its carousel ad, as we predicted in H3. Thus, popular brands can benefit especially from carousel ad formats.
