These findings also resonate with evidence of the strong impacts of brand attitudes on consumer behavior (Gresham and Shimp <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0023" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1985</a></span>; Rietveld et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0052" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>).</p></div></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0007"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e1073">General discussion</h2><p>To investigate the effectiveness of carousel ads, a prominent newsfeed format on social media, we conducted a multimethod investigation, focused on two key outcomes: attention and brand recall. Across four studies, including qualitative interviews, mobile eye-tracking, an online experiment, and a videography field study, we demonstrate that carousel ads significantly increase advertising effectiveness, measured as attention and brand recall. <button class="ref show-table-fig-ref" data-id="t0002" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table" data-registered="">Table 2</button> provides an overview of the studies and findings.</p><div class="tableView"><div class="tableCaption"><div class="short-legend"><h3><p class="captionText"><span class="captionLabel">Table 2. </span> Overview of studies and main findings.</p></h3></div></div><div class="tableDownloadOption" id="t0002-table-wrapper"><a class="downloadButton btn btn-sm" role="button" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/action/downloadTable?id=t0002&doi=10.1080%2F02650487.2026.2624918&downloadType=CSV">Download CSV</a><a data-id="t0002" class="downloadButton btn btn-sm displaySizeTable" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" role="button" data-behaviour="show-popup" data-popup-event-type="table" data-registered="">Display Table</a></div></div><p>Study 1 reveals how carousel ads create a unique user experience characterized by four experiential stages: curiosity, convenience, self-control, and immersion. Study 2 demonstrates that activated carousel ads increase attention and brand recall compared with other ad formats, such as image, video, and collection ads. Furthermore, with Study 2 we find that longer carousel ads lead to greater attention and more fixations. However, brands only benefit from the carousel effect if their carousels get activated. Thus, in Studies 3a and 3b, we investigate how brand attitudes can drive carousel activation. The findings align with the attitude–behavior consistency framework (Fazio and Zanna <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0018" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1981</a></span>; Kraus <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0035" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1995</a></span>), showing that consumers are significantly more likely to activate carousel ads posted by strong brands. Moreover, the results provide empirical evidence that, in social media settings, stronger brands benefit from not only increased engagement (Rietveld et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0052" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>) but also opt-in, exploratory behaviors such as swiping through an ad sequence. These findings contribute to both theory and practice by clarifying the mechanisms by which interactivity and brand perceptions influence consumer behavior on social media platforms.</p><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0007-S2001"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e1173">Theoretical implications</h3><p>Our findings contribute to advertising and social media theory in several ways. First, we provide new empirical insights into how and why carousel ads work. Our research complements advertising research by introducing the <i>carousel effect</i>, an immersive, user-driven interaction facilitated by perceived control and narrative structure, as a mechanism for enhancing attention and brand recall. As an extension of existing advertising response models, we propose incorporating voluntary, opt-in behavior and sequential navigation.</p><p>Second, we identify four experiential stages that sequentially shape consumers’ interactions with carousel ads: curiosity, convenience, self-control, and immersion. These stages link core psychological constructs to ad effectiveness and provide a structured account of how consumers move from initial exposure to deeper message engagement. Our results confirm earlier findings that control over the ad experience improves user engagement and satisfaction (Hu and Wise <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0027" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Liu and Shrum <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0038" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2002</a></span>); they also align with evidence from Lim and Childs (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0037" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>) that narrative content can enhance immersion in social media environments.</p><p>Third, the results demonstrate that activated carousel ads generate significantly longer attention spans than other in-feed ad formats. These effects are consistent with prior eye-tracking studies that establish strong links between attention metrics (e.g. gaze duration, fixations) and memory performance (Boerman and Müller <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0007" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2022</a></span>; Rosbergen, Pieters, and Wedel <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0054" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1997</a></span>); they also affirm Guitart, Hervet, and Hildebrand’s (2019) assertion that increased attention can predict brand recognition in mobile environments. This effect increases with ad length, in support of theories related to interactive and narrative engagement in persuasive contexts (Phillips and McQuarrie <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0047" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2010</a></span>; Van Laer et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0065" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2014</a></span>). As Heitmayer and Lahlou (<span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0026" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2021</a></span>) propose, swiping-based mobile interfaces, as “cognition attractors,” can prolong engagement, because they support continuous, low-effort interactions. In this sense, the swipe-based interaction is more than a design feature; it constitutes a behavioral mechanism that shapes advertising effectiveness, through consumer agency, self-paced exploration, and perceived control (Hu and Wise <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0027" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Skinner <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0059" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1996</a></span>). As a contribution to research into online advertising effectiveness (e.g. Briggs and Hollis <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0009" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1997</a></span>; Huang et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0028" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Liu-Thompkins <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0039" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2019</a></span>), we identify the critical influence of sideways swiping through carousel ads on in-feed ad format interactions and resulting attention.</p><p class="last">Fourth, we establish that brand attitude significantly predicts carousel ad activation, in line with evidence that brand attitudes predict attention and engagement in both digital and physical environments (Bialkova, Grunert, and van Trijp <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0006" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>; Rietveld et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0052" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>). Consumers are more likely to activate ads from popular brands, so carousel effectiveness depends on both the design of the format and brand perceptions, in line with research that cites the powerful influence of brand attitudes on consumer behavior (Gresham and Shimp <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0023" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>1985</a></span>; Rietveld et al. <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0052" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2020</a></span>).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0007-S2002"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e1238">Managerial implications</h3><p>For advertisers seeking to improve their ad effectiveness in crowded social media environments, we highlight carousel ads as a high-impact, low-risk option. They can capture significant attention and generate stronger brand recall, without incurring any more media costs than static or video formats (Meta <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0042" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2024</a></span>). The marginal production cost of additional images is minimal, particularly given recent advances in AI-enabled ad creation tools (e.g. AICarousels.com <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0001" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>; Canva <span class="ref-lnk lazy-ref bibr"><a data-rid="CIT0010" href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/02650487.2026.2624918#" data-behaviour="toggle-ref" data-ref-type="bibr" data-label="reference" data-registered=""><span class="off-screen">Citation</span>2025</a></span>), which lower production barriers even more.</p><p>Strong brands in particular can benefit from the carousel effect. Brand managers working for established brands should prioritize carousel ads over other in-feed formats. However, even if strong brands naturally benefit from a greater activation likelihood, new or lesser-known brands still can leverage the carousel effect, such as by creating a compelling first card, featuring vivid colors and emotional cues, and including storytelling hooks that spark curiosity and prompt sideways swiping. Without such user-initiated sideways swiping, the performance of carousel ads is comparable to that of other in-feed ad formats. Therefore, maximizing the appeal of the first card is particularly critical. Once activated, longer carousel ads also lead to longer attention spans, so advertisers should make strategic use of the ad format’s capacity by including more cards, while still ensuring the content remains relevant and engaging.</p><p class="last">With their multi-card structure, carousel ads are well-suited for narrative storytelling and product walkthroughs. Guiding users through a sequence of visuals and messages can create immersive experiences that unfold like a mini-campaign. As technical and creative constraints continue to diminish, carousel ads offer increasingly compelling opportunities for brands to cut through the clutter in social media newsfeeds and generate more effective advertising to attract consumers’ attention.</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_2" id="S0007-S2003"><h3 class="section-heading-3" id="d1e1253">Limitations and further research</h3><p class="last">This study provides novel insights into the effectiveness of carousel ads but also is subject to several limitations that might be addressed by further research. First, we conducted Study 2 in a real-world setting and thus could not control the advertising content. A laboratory experiment with standardized newsfeeds could elaborate on our findings; for example, it might explore brand recognition as a less complex but still relevant variable, particularly for inducing recognition-based purchase decisions. In addition, although the use of mobile eye tracking in Study 2 may have raised concerns about potential reactivity effects, the observed swiping behavior closely mirrored the self-reported, habitual usage patterns documented in Study 1. This consistency suggests that reactivity is unlikely to drive the observed effects. Nonetheless, future research could further corroborate this conclusion, for example by combining attention tracking with longer acclimatization periods or other unobtrusive measurement approaches. Second, we find that positive brand attitudes increase the likelihood of carousel ad activation; additional research is needed to detail how new or lesser-known brands can encourage swiping. For example, studies should address which characteristics of the first card (e.g. vivid colors, human elements, photographic style, content type) influence activation rates most effectively. Third, we introduce narrative storytelling as a key affordance of carousel ads, but we hope continued work will test the impact of structured storytelling elements explicitly. Applying existing storytelling frameworks, such as beginning–middle–end sequencing, thematic consistency, suspense, or narrative surprise, could reveal further insights into narrative transportation and its persuasive impact. Fourth, our data indicate that longer carousel ads receive more attention, but platform-imposed constraints (e.g. Instagram’s 20-card limit) prevent us from testing for the upper thresholds of this effect. Research exploring if and when this attention benefit plateaus or reverses could help determine optimal carousel lengths. Fifth, we predict that the findings of our studies, conducted on Instagram and Facebook, generalize to other newsfeed-based social media platforms that host carousel ads. However, platforms like TikTok or LinkedIn differ in their feed architecture and the content expectations and behaviors they evoke from consumers. Comparing carousel ad effectiveness across platforms could provide more strategic guidance for advertisers. By addressing such questions, researchers can refine the proposed carousel effect and bridge persistent gaps in our understanding of digital interaction patterns and advertising effectiveness.</p></div></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0009"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e1257">Ethical approval</h2><p class="last">We conducted this research at the University of Wuppertal, Germany. We followed the ethical guidelines and standards set forth by the institution. As our studies did not involve sensitive data or potentially harmful manipulations, formal institutional review board (IRB) approval was not required by the University of Wuppertal.</p></div><div class="pb-dropzone" data-pb-dropzone="scholixLinksDropZone"><!-- Empty dropzone --></div><div id="coi-statement" class="NLM_sec"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e1260">Disclosure statement</h2><p class="last">No potential conflict of interest was reported by the author(s).</p></div><div class="NLM_sec NLM_sec_level_1" id="S0010"><h2 class="section-heading-2" id="d1e1263">Data availability statement</h2><p class="last">Due to its proprietary nature, the data set used in this study cannot be made openly available.</p></div></div><script nonce="a38636514dc5163f-LAX">tandf.tfviewerdata={"table-index-map":{"t0001":0,"t0002":1},"tables":[{"settings":{"hasCsvFormat":true},"content":"<div id=\"table-content-t0001\"><table class=\"topbot\"><caption><div class=\"paragraph\"><p class=\"captionText\"><span class=\"captionLabel\">Table 1. <\/span> Example ad format evaluations.<\/p><\/div><\/caption><thead><tr><th align=\"left\"><i>Ad Format<\/i><\/th><th align=\"center\"><i>Example Statements<\/i><\/th><th align=\"center\"><i>Participants<\/i><\/th><\/tr><\/thead><tbody><tr><td align=\"left\">Carousel<\/td><td align=\"left\">I like it more than a video, because it’s not so intrusive and doesn’t suddenly make a lot of noise.
